rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections <U+2013> the study runs its own coupled SWAP<U+2013>C2VSim hydro-economic model of a 3-year drought scenario for the Central Valley and reports its own estimates of fallowing, revenue losses, pumping costs and regional employment effects (Tables 3<U+2013>7); it also compiles Landsat/MODIS NDVI idle-land estimates (Table 8).
rows.notes: The study's own subject is groundwater pumping as a drought buffer analysed with a hydro-economic model; remote sensing appears only as an ancillary cross-check. Section 'Estimates of agricultural idle land' and Table 8 compare SWAP-modelled idle land with NASA (NDVI, 95% classification accuracy against 670 field sites) and UC Davis Landsat estimates, finding similar ranges for the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys and a wider spread for Tulare Lake Basin. The Discussion states that remotely sensed data are helpful for refining model calibration and that further work on using remote sensing to recalibrate the optimization model is needed. The study thus shows remote sensing can detect/confirm the extent of drought-idled land (a precondition), but it does not evaluate remote sensing as an instrument for water policy or risk management against scarcity, climate change or competing demands, which is what the passage claims. Hence Q2 is 'no' and the row is marked upstream.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is a modelling case study of the 2014 California drought; remote sensing is used only to corroborate modelled idle-land estimates, not as the technology under evaluation.
